references.text: The description of humanity's condition before the flood in [ref:1 Mos 6:1-7|Genesis 6:1-7] forms the background for Jesus' words that people were eating, drinking, and marrying without paying attention to the coming judgment.
[ref:1 Mos 7:7|Genesis 7:7] tells us that Noah entered the ark, as Jesus refers to it: "until the day when Noah entered the ark".
[ref:1 Mos 7:10-24|Genesis 7:10-24] describes the flood itself that came and destroyed all living things, which Jesus summarizes with "the flood came and destroyed them all".
In [ref:1 Mos 7:1|Genesis 7:1], God commands Noah to enter the ark, the specific event Jesus points to as the turning point before judgment fell.

God's announcement of the coming destruction and His command to Noah to build the ark in [ref:1 Mos 6:13-18|Genesis 6:13-18] shows that judgment was foretold, while people lived their lives without repentance.
[ref:Matt 24:37-39|Matthew 24:37-39] is the parallel passage where Jesus uses the same example of Noah's days – people were eating, drinking, and marrying until the flood came and took them all away.

[ref:2 Pet 2:5|2 Peter 2:5] mentions that God did not spare the ancient world but preserved Noah as a preacher of righteousness when He brought the flood upon the ungodly – an example of God's judgment to which Jesus refers here.

[ref:Hebr 11:7|Hebrews 11:7] highlights Noah's faith as he built the ark to save his household, while the rest of the world was condemned – the same contrast between salvation and judgment that Jesus draws attention to.

[ref:1 Pet 3:20|1 Peter 3:20] refers to those who were disobedient in Noah's days while the ark was being built, and only eight souls were saved through water – a motif that underscores Jesus' point about the unpreparedness of many.

The preceding verse [ref:Luk 17:26|Luke 17:26] introduces the comparison: "Just as it was in Noah's days, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man", which verse 27 expands on with concrete details.
[ref:Luk 17:28-30|Luke 17:28-30] gives a parallel example from Lot's days in Sodom, where people also lived their daily lives without expecting judgment, just as in Noah's days.
In [ref:Jes 54:9|Isaiah 54:9], God refers to Noah's flood as a historical judgment He has sworn not to repeat, confirming the significance of the flood narrative as a pattern of God's judgment.
